+

Identifiers & names

+

+ A bare identifier — a path segment or a helper name — may be almost any + character. Only whitespace and this reserved set are off-limits bare: +

+

{t("! \" # % & ' ( ) * + , . / ; < = > @ [ \\ ] ^ ` { | } ~")}

+

+ So letters, digits, _, $, -, + : and ? are all fine bare: kebab-case keys like + {t("{{first-name}}")} and Ruby/Mustache-style predicate keys like + {t("{{active?}}")} need no ceremony. The reserved characters carry + structural meaning instead — . and / separate path + segments, @ prefixes data variables + ({t("{{@index}}")}, {t("{{@root}}")}), and the rest are + operators or grouping. +

+

Anything else: [segment literals]

+

+ Wrap a key in square brackets to use characters that aren't bare-legal — + spaces, dots, or reserved punctuation. This is the escape hatch: +

+ + + + + + + +
NeedWrite
a key with a space{t("{{[full name]}}")}
a bracketed segment inside a path{t("{{address.[street name]}}")}
a key with reserved punctuation{t("{{[a+b]}}")}
+

+ Names that look like literals are literals, not lookups: + true, false, null, numbers, and quoted + {t("\"strings\"")} — use the bracket form + ({t("{{[true]}}")}) if you really have a key named true. +

+

@@ -143,6 +143,17 @@ $ ~> | $ | {

+

Names are just keys

+

+ Mustache has no identifier grammar. A name is the tag's text, trimmed, looked + up as a literal key in your data — so almost anything works: + {t("{{first-name}}")}, {t("{{active?}}")}, even + {t("{{2nd}}")}. The only characters a bare name can't contain are + whitespace, . (the segment separator, below) and the active + delimiters {t("{{ }}")}. Nesting is the one bit of structure: a + dot splits the lookup into a path. +

+

Dotted names

Reach into nested objects with dots: {t("{{name.first}}")}.
